title: Shloka 182
subtitle: The thousandth name, and the line that closes the singing

lines.deva: एवं श्रीललिता देव्या नाम्नां साहस्रकं जगुः
lines.iast: evaṃ śrīlalitā devyā nāmnāṃ sāhasrakaṃ jaguḥ

word.translation: Thus — pointing back over all eighteen hundred and some syllables that have just been recited.

morphology.note: Indeclinables take no endings. The final m appears here as anusvāra because a sibilant follows: evam + śrī → evaṃ śrī.

word.note: The word that turns the preceding thousand names into a completed object. Everything before this line was the hymn; from here the text speaks about the hymn.

word.translation: …belonging to the goddess Śrī Lalitā, whose name the hymn has just finished pronouncing for the thousandth time.

morphology.note: Carries no ending of its own: it is the prior member of a compound whose case is supplied at the far end, by devyāḥ.

children.gloss: light, splendour, prosperity; as a prefix to a name, an honorific
playful, charming, lovely — from √lal, to play or sport; her proper name

word.note: Printed as a separate word, but grammatically it is bound to devyāḥ: the two together are one compound in the genitive. The same name closed the thousand two words earlier as lalitāmbikā, so it is heard twice in a single line — once as the last of the names, once as the owner of them all.

word.translation: …of the goddess — the genitive that the whole line hangs from.

morphology.note: The genitive singular of devī is devyāḥ. The visarga is not missing: final -āḥ regularly loses it before a voiced sound, and nāmnāṃ begins with n, so devyāḥ nāmnāṃ is written devyā nāmnāṃ.

word.note: Worth pausing on, because the written form devyā is identical to the instrumental singular and is easily misread as "by the goddess" — which would make her the singer rather than the subject. The singers are plural, and named by the verb at the end of the line.

word.translation: …of the names — all of them, taken together.

morphology.note: Weak stem nāmn- plus the genitive plural -ām gives nāmnām, written with anusvāra before the following s: nāmnāṃ sāhasrakam.

word.note: A partitive genitive depending on sāhasrakam: not "the thousand names" as a loose phrase but "the thousand-fold collection of the names". Sanskrit is being precise about the fact that the thousand is a grouping imposed on the names, which is why the count can be a matter of argument at all.

word.translation: …the full thousand of them, as one thing.

morphology.note: A secondary derivative: sahasra, a thousand, with vṛddhi of the first vowel and the suffix -ka, giving a noun for the collection rather than the number.

word.note: The object of the verb, and singular — they did not sing a thousand names, they sang one thousand-fold thing. That grammatical choice is the reason the hymn is treated in practice as a single unbreakable recitation rather than a list one may sample from.

word.translation: …they sang. The hymn's last word puts the whole of it in the past tense and in someone else's mouth.

morphology.rootMeaning: to sing, chant, recite in song
morphology.note: Reduplicated perfect of √gai: the root vowel weakens and the reduplicating syllable ja- is prefixed, giving jagau in the third singular and jaguḥ in the third plural.

word.note: Plural, and no subject is stated, because the subject was established when the hymn began: the eight Vāgdevatās, the goddesses of speech, who were commissioned to compose it. The last act of the text is to disown its own authorship — it does not say "I have praised you" but "thus they sang", so that the reciter joins a performance already under way rather than starting one.

namas.translation: Her fame reaches everyone, from small children to herdsmen, and asks no learning of those who receive it.

compound.gloss: known to all alike, children and cowherds included

children.gloss: reaching as far as children and cowherds
as far as, up to and including

namas.translation: Her order stands over everyone, and nobody has the standing to step across it.

compound.gloss: she whose rule no one can overstep

children.gloss: not to be transgressed by anyone
to be leapt over, to be transgressed

namas.translation: The Śrīcakra, first among all diagrams, is the house she lives in.

compound.gloss: she whose abode is the royal Śrīcakra

namas.translation: She is the beautiful one of the three cities, and the honorific śrīmat marks this as the name under which the whole tradition knows her.

compound.gloss: the illustrious beauty of the triple city

children.gloss: the beautiful one of the three cities

namas.translation: She is Śrī and Śivā at once, radiant prosperity and quiet beatitude held in one name, the feminine of auspiciousness itself.

compound.gloss: she who is Śrī and equally Śivā

children.gloss: radiance, prosperity, majesty; the goddess Śrī
the auspicious one, the feminine of Śiva

namas.translation: Her form is the single fact of Śiva and Śakti being one, and the stotra ends by saying not that she is a partner in that union but that she is the union.

morphology.note: The last of the -rūpiṇī names is analysed like the rest: -in supplies the possession, so śivaśaktyaikyarūpa is the compound and rūpiṇī is formed on it. The bahuvrīhi sense, she who has the union of Śiva and Śakti for her form, is the familiar alternative.

compound.gloss: having the oneness of Śiva and Śakti for her form

children.gloss: the oneness of Śiva and Śakti
Śiva, the auspicious, the quiescent ground

namas.translation: The last of the thousand gathers all the rest into a single address: Lalitā, the one at play, who is Mother.

children.gloss: Lalitā, the graceful one, she who is at play

commentary.meaning: Seven names, and then the end. The first two say that she is known to everyone, down to children and cowherds, and that her command cannot be stepped across by anyone — universal recognition and unconditional authority, laid side by side. Then three names in a row open with śrī, exactly as the hymn's first verse of names opened with three: her dwelling is the sovereign Śrīcakra, the name under which the tradition knows her is Tripurasundarī, and she is Śrī and Śivā in one word. The last two say what the thousand has been moving towards. She is not a partner in the union of Śiva and Śakti; her form is that union. And then, at one thousand, the hymn puts down its technical vocabulary and says Lalitā, mother. What follows is not a name at all. Thus, the text reports, they sang the thousand names of the goddess Śrī Lalitā — a plural verb in the past tense. The last thing the hymn does is attribute itself to someone else.
commentary.history:
The half-line that ends this module is a frame, not a name, and it marks a seam in a longer text. The thousand names are embedded in the Lalitopākhyāna, the long narrative section of the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa in which the sage Hayagrīva recites to Agastya, and after this line Hayagrīva keeps talking. What follows is the phalaśruti, literally the hearing of the fruit: verses that tell Agastya what recitation of the thousand names accomplishes, when it should be done, and for whom. Most printed editions include those verses, and many recitations chant them. This presentation ends where the names end, which is a defensible place to stop and also an incomplete one, and a reader should know that the text continues.

Almost every hymn of this kind ends that way, and it is worth understanding why rather than treating it as an embarrassment appended to something finer. A phalaśruti does at least three jobs. It is a colophon in verse, telling a listener that the recitation is over — useful in a culture where texts were heard rather than seen and had no last page. It is a rubric, prescribing when and how often and in what condition the text should be used, which is the only place such instructions could live. And it is a claim about what kind of thing the text is: not a description of the goddess to be assessed for accuracy, but an act that does something when performed. There is a fourth and less elevated function that honest scholarship has also noted, which is advertisement. Such passages commended a text to patrons and communities in a crowded field, and their language of unlimited benefit belongs partly to that competition.

How a modern reader should take the promises is a real question and deserves better than the two easy answers. Credulity treats the specific claims as a schedule of payments and is generally disappointed. Embarrassment treats all of it as metaphor for inner transformation, which sounds sophisticated but is an imposition, because the texts plainly mean some of it literally and the traditions that carried them have always contained people who tested the claims and stayed. The commentators themselves use both registers and switch between them without apology, reading an extravagant promise figuratively and a modest one literally, according to what the passage seems to be doing. Perhaps the most useful way in is to notice what a phalaśruti asks for in exchange. What it prescribes is repetition over years, at fixed times, in a settled condition of mind — and the previous verse of this very hymn has just named her as one who becomes known through practice carried past the ordinary measure. Whatever else the promises are, they are a description of what the tradition believes such a life produces, made by people who had watched it happen.

The closing names are arranged with obvious care. The thousand opens with śrīmātā, Śrī the mother, followed by two more names beginning with śrī; it closes with three names beginning with śrī, and then with lalitāmbikā, Lalitā the mother. The hymn ends where it began, on the same word, with the same prefix ringing three times on either side. There is a further echo worth catching: lalita, from a root meaning to play or to dally, means the one at play, and five verses back the hymn called her līlāvinodinī, she who diverts herself in play. The name that gives the whole text its title has been waiting at position one thousand, and what it means is what the hymn said about her when it came down into the domestic room near the end.

The last line then does something no other line in the thousand does. Jaguḥ is the third person plural of the perfect of √gai, to sing: they sang. The plural is not vague. In the frame of the purāṇa the hymn is composed and sung by the vāgdevatās, the goddesses of speech headed by Vaśinī, who are named as the seers of this stotra in the ritual preliminaries that precede any formal recitation of it. So the last act of the text is to step back and report that the singing was done by someone else, in front of the goddess, before any of us arrived. Sāhasrakam, formed from sahasra with the lengthening that makes a derived noun, means the set of a thousand taken as one thing. The genitive in this line is loosely written — one expects devyāḥ where the printed text has devyā — and the sense is not in question, but it is the kind of small irregularity that is worth noticing rather than smoothing over.
commentary.practice:
The last two quarters of the hymn are also its hardest to say. Sarvānullaṅghyaśāsanā contains ll and then ṅghy, a guttural nasal, an aspirated guttural, and a palatal glide in a single cluster, which is about as much as Sanskrit asks of a tongue anywhere. Take it slowly: sar-vā-nul-laṅ-ghya-śā-sa-nā, with both l sounds sounded and the ṅ made at the back where the gh is made. Śrīmattripurasundarī has ttri, a doubled dental followed by r, and the doubling must be heard or the honorific śrīmat disappears. And śivaśaktyaikyarūpiṇī has ktyai, three consonants running into a full diphthong, followed at once by kya. Get these wrong and the two most important names in the verse are unrecognisable.

Against that, the three śrī names give the ear something to hold. Sound all three parts of śrī — palatal ś, then r, then long ī — and the pattern of the closing line becomes audible as a pattern rather than as a difficulty.

For archanā the seven datives are ābālagopaviditāyai, sarvānullaṅghyaśāsanāyai, śrīcakrarājanilayāyai, śrīmattripurasundaryai, śrīśivāyai, śivaśaktyaikyarūpiṇyai, and lalitāmbikāyai. The last of these is the thousandth offering, and in most household and temple practice it is the point at which the flowers or the rice in the hand are finished and something is done to mark the close — an āratī, a final prostration, a period of sitting without speech. The closing half-line is not offered with namaḥ. It is the one place in the recitation where you are not addressing her but saying what has occurred, and it should be chanted plainly, in the same metre and at the same pace, without dropping into an announcer's voice.

What it means to have arrived here is worth stating carefully. Nothing in the hymn's last verse congratulates the reciter. It says instead that she is known to children and to cowherds, which is placed directly after a verse saying she is known only through practice carried past the ordinary measure. A person who has just spent thirty minutes on a thousand difficult names is being told, in the first four syllables of the final verse, that the knowledge in question was never rationed to the people who could pronounce them. That is not a rebuke of the effort. It is a correction of what the effort was for.

And then the text hands itself away. The last verb is plural and in the past: they sang. Whoever is reciting is not the author of this and is not its first speaker; the position offered is that of someone repeating what eight goddesses of speech said in front of the one they were describing. This is the reason the tradition treats the end of the hymn as a place to begin again rather than as a finish line. What the hymn asks of a person who has come to the end of the thousand names is not a conclusion drawn or a state attained. It is that he should have somewhere to be tomorrow at the same hour, and that when he sits down there he should remember that the last name of the thousand was not a definition but a form of address: mother.

crossReferences.deva: शिवः शक्त्या युक्तो यदि भवति शक्तः प्रभवितुं न चेदेवं देवो न खलु कुशलः स्पन्दितुमपि । अतस्त्वामाराध्यां हरिहरविरिञ्चादिभिरपि प्रणन्तुं स्तोतुं वा कथमकृतपुण्यः प्रभवति ॥
crossReferences.iast: śivaḥ śaktyā yukto yadi bhavati śaktaḥ prabhavituṃ na ced evaṃ devo na khalu kuśalaḥ spanditum api | atas tvām ārādhyāṃ hariharaviriñcādibhir api praṇantuṃ stotuṃ vā katham akṛtapuṇyaḥ prabhavati ||
crossReferences.translation: Śiva is able to create only when he is joined with Śakti; without that, the god is not competent even to stir. So how should a man who has laid up no merit be capable of bowing to you, or of praising you, whom Hari and Hara and Viriñci themselves worship?
crossReferences.relevance: The most direct statement in the literature of what śivaśaktyaikyarūpiṇī claims, and the reason the name is not a courtesy paid to a consort: without the union there is not even motion, so the union is not an event that happens to two things but the condition of anything happening at all. The second half of the verse is the right note on which to finish a thousand names, since it questions whether praising her was ever within the praiser's competence.

crossReferences.source: Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.4 (the same line returns at the end of the second chapter)
crossReferences.deva: यतो वाचो निवर्तन्ते अप्राप्य मनसा सह । आनन्दं ब्रह्मणो विद्वान्न बिभेति कुतश्चन ॥
crossReferences.iast: yato vāco nivartante aprāpya manasā saha | ānandaṃ brahmaṇo vidvān na bibheti kutaścana ||
crossReferences.translation: That from which words turn back, together with the mind, having failed to reach it — one who knows the bliss of brahman is afraid of nothing at all.
crossReferences.relevance: The necessary corrective at the end of a thousand words. The Upaniṣad does not say that speech is forbidden or useless; it says that speech goes out and comes back without having arrived, and that what is known anyway is enough to end fear. Reading it here explains why the hymn's last name is not its most technical one but its plainest, and why the text stops rather than concluding.

crossReferences.source: Devī Māhātmya 5 (the refrain of the hymn beginning "yā devī sarvabhūteṣu")
crossReferences.deva: या देवी सर्वभूतेषु मातृरूपेण संस्थिता । नमस्तस्यै नमस्तस्यै नमस्तस्यै नमो नमः ॥
crossReferences.iast: yā devī sarvabhūteṣu mātṛrūpeṇa saṃsthitā | namas tasyai namas tasyai namas tasyai namo namaḥ ||
crossReferences.translation: The goddess who abides in all beings in the form of the mother — homage to her, homage to her, homage to her, homage and homage again.
crossReferences.relevance: The other great litany of the goddess arrives at the same place by the opposite method. Where the sahasranāma piles up a thousand distinct epithets and ends by dropping all of them for the word mother, the Devī Māhātmya names one form at a time and then abandons description altogether in favour of repeated homage. Both texts treat mātṛ as the term that does not need to be improved on, which is worth knowing when you reach lalitāmbikā.

references.title: The Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa, translated and annotated
references.author: tr. G. V. Tagare, Ancient Indian Tradition and Mythology series (Motilal Banarsidass)
references.note: The frame this hymn sits inside. Read the Lalitopākhyāna to see who Hayagrīva and Agastya are, why the thousand names are being recited to a sage in the first place, and what Hayagrīva goes on to say after the half-line that ends this module. Nothing else in English gives you the whole setting, and the setting is what the closing line refers to.

references.title: Encountering the Goddess: A Translation of the Devī-Māhātmya and a Study of Its Interpretation
references.author: Thomas B. Coburn (SUNY Press, 1991)
references.note: The best treatment in English of how a Sanskrit goddess text has actually been used, including a serious discussion of the verses of promised benefit that such texts end with — what they claim, who repeated them, and how communities took them. Coburn neither ridicules the claims nor pretends they are only symbolic, which is the model for reading a phalaśruti honestly.

references.title: Hindu Tantric and Śākta Literature
references.author: Teun Goudriaan and Sanjukta Gupta (Otto Harrassowitz, 1981)
references.note: A survey rather than a study, and the place to find out how many texts of this shape exist. Its value here is perspective: the thousand-name hymn is a genre with hundreds of members, and seeing this one as a member of it makes both its conventions and its individual quality easier to judge.

references.title: Śrī Lalitā Sahasranāma, with introduction and translation
references.author: Swami Tapasyananda (Sri Ramakrishna Math, Madras)
references.note: A compact single-volume edition with the Sanskrit, a plain English rendering, and the closing sections that follow the thousand names. Useful precisely at this point, because it lets you read past the last name and see for yourself what the text promises rather than taking anyone's summary of it.

references.title: Śrī Lalitā Sahasranāma (recorded recitation)
references.author: M. S. Subbulakshmi (HMV / Saregama)
references.note: Worth returning to at the end for one specific reason. The closing half-line is in the same metre as the thousand names and is chanted the same way, so the transition from the last name to the statement that the names have been sung passes almost without a seam. Hearing that is the quickest way to understand that the frame is part of the text rather than a note about it.
